# Kaleidoscope

> Local memory for coding agents. Your agent forgets everything between sessions; Kaleidoscope gives it a memory that lives in a folder on your own machine and is shared by every editor and agent you use. Install it with `npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope`. It needs a key to run — email contact@kleosresearch.xyz.

- [Documentation](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/): what Kaleidoscope is, and which page answers your question
- [Getting started](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/getting-started/): install, activate with your key, and give a project a memory
- [Give your agent the skill](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/skill/): how an agent is told Kaleidoscope exists, and the four files it installs
- [Install](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/packages/): the package names and what is inside them
- [CLI reference](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/): every `kscope` command and flag
- [MCP reference](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/mcp/): the two tools an agent sees, `search` and `remember`, and how to call them
- [Integrations](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/): Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, LangChain, LangGraph, Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI, and any standard MCP client
- [Security](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/security/): what is isolated from what, what is not signed, and how to report a vulnerability
- [Privacy](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/privacy/): what stays on your machine, where a credential would be kept, and what this website itself does
- [Licenses and terms](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/legal/): Apache-2.0 and CC BY 4.0 are in force; the product terms are reviewed drafts, not yet adopted
- [Privacy notice](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/legal/privacy-notice/): a counsel-reviewed draft of the production privacy terms, not yet in force
- [Security policy](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/legal/security-policy/): a counsel-reviewed draft of the disclosure and supported-version policy, not yet in force
- [Support policy](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/legal/support-policy/): a counsel-reviewed draft of the support scope and response targets, not yet in force
- [Account](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/account/): you do not need an account, and you cannot create one yet
- [Operations](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/operations/): back up your memory, move it, uninstall, and delete a vault safely
- [Platforms](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/compatibility/): which platforms Kaleidoscope is for, and the one thing Windows does differently
- [Benchmarks](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/benchmarks/): two separate experiments — on the larger corpus, twelve times the memories at the same answer quality; on the smaller one, level with mem0 at 24% fewer tokens
- [Status](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/status/): whether anything is available, whether anything is down, and what has actually been run
- [Public agent skill](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/SKILL.md): how an agent should retrieve and write memory
- [Agent instructions](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/agent-instructions.md): the short pointers Kaleidoscope installs into AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or a Cursor rule
- [Status record](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/status.json): the same status these pages state, in machine-readable form
- [Platform support record](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/platform-support.json): which platforms have been run on and which have only had a compiler check
- [Full CLI help text](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/reference/kaleidoscope-cli.txt): the complete `kaleidoscope` help output
- [Tool reference](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/reference/kaleidoscope-mcp.json): the fields of the two tools an agent sees

Kaleidoscope is installable today: `npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope` gives you the `kscope` command on macOS and Linux, on both Apple Silicon and x86_64. It needs a key to run. We send keys by email — write to contact@kleosresearch.xyz. Windows is not supported: creating a vault there is refused on purpose until the filesystem work lands.

Once it is installed, `kscope init` in a project creates the memory and connects whichever agent you use. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, standard MCP clients and the agent frameworks all read the same vault. Two of those connections have a limit worth stating: Codex's configuration entry is written and removed exactly, but Codex offers no way to confirm it then starts the server, and Cursor's has never been checked by launching Cursor itself. The agent frameworks were tested against stand-in models rather than a live provider.

What is not here: hosted memory does not exist -- there is no service, endpoint, API or waitlist, and nothing syncs your memory anywhere. It stays in a folder in your project. Apache-2.0 covers the public code and CC BY 4.0 covers this documentation, and both are in force; the engine licence, privacy notice, security policy and support policy have been reviewed by counsel but not adopted, so none of them is yet in force and there is no support commitment. Nothing is signed for release. The part that stores and searches your memory ships as proprietary object code, and its source is not public. Benchmark results are described in plain words on the benchmarks page; the full benchmark method is not published yet.

---

# Kaleidoscope

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Local memory for agents · one vault · every tool

  Your agent forgets. This is where it remembers.

  Every session your coding agent starts from nothing. It re-asks what you answered, re-reads code it understood, and repeats mistakes you already paid for.

  Kaleidoscope gives it a memory that stays on your machine and follows you between tools. Your agent gets two tools: look something up, and write something down.

    Get started
    Give your agent the skill
    What works today

## Install it

```bash
npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope
export KALEIDOSCOPE_API_KEY=<your key>
kscope activate
cd ~/your-project && kscope init
```

Restart your editor, then ask it what you decided last week.

No key yet? Email
contact@kleosresearch.xyz.
Getting started walks the same four steps slowly.

## What you get

**It stays on your machine.** Your memory is a folder inside your project,
served by a process on your laptop. Nothing is uploaded.

**One memory, every tool.** Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode read the
same vault. What your agent learned in one is there in the next.

**Your agent drives it.** `kscope init` wires whichever editors you already
have. After that you talk normally, and it decides when to read and when to
write.

## Where to go next

| | |
|---|---|
| Getting started | Install, activate, give a project a memory |
| Give your agent the skill | Teach an agent to use its memory well |
| Editors and agents | Find yours |
| What works today | Platforms and tools we have run |
| Documentation | Everything else |

# Kaleidoscope documentation

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Kaleidoscope is local memory for agents. Memories live in a vault on your
machine, and every editor you connect reads that vault through one command,
`kscope`.

```bash
npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope
```

Running it needs a key — email
contact@kleosresearch.xyz. There is no
account to create and no sign-in.

# Account and devices

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/account/
Updated: 2026-08-30

You do not need an account to use Kaleidoscope — your memory lives on your
machine and works without one. You also could not sign in today if you wanted
to: every command that reaches the account service answers
`provider not configured`, because no sign-in service is configured or
published.

## What signing in would be for

Signing in is designed as an ordinary browser sign-in, with a code-based path
for machines that have no browser. It manages your product account and the
devices attached to it. It is not a connection to hosted memory: no hosted
service, endpoint, API, waitlist, or sync path exists, and signing in would not
opt you into one.

## What it never does to your memory

Signing in never uploads, syncs, analyses, trains on, or deletes your memory.
Memory content, your queries, the results you got back, memory IDs, graph data,
local paths, and vault locations are all excluded from the account protocol, and
the account client rejects those fields — and any absolute local path — before
anything would leave your machine.

## Where a sign-in credential would be kept

Signing in is not built yet, so nothing is stored anywhere today. When it is,
the refresh credential goes to the operating system's own credential store — the
login Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, the Secret Service on
Linux — and never into a file we write, into an editor's configuration, or into
a profile. On Linux, if no secret service is running, signing in stops and tells
you rather than falling back to something weaker.

One caveat we would rather state than let you discover: on macOS, whether the
system remembers your approval depends on the program being signed with a stable
identity. Kaleidoscope is not signed for release,
so an unsigned build can be asked for your login password every time it reaches
the Keychain. That is a property of unsigned software, not of how the credential
is stored, and it goes away when signed builds ship.

Signing in is only ever about your account and your devices. It does not upload,
sync, analyse, train on or delete your memory, and it does not connect you to a
hosted service — there isn't one.

An **alpha key is not a sign-in and does not use the Keychain at all.** It is
read from an environment variable or from a file you write yourself, and it
never prompts for your login password. See
if you have an alpha key.

## What logging out changes

Logging out removes or revokes your credentials, according to the scope you
chose. It does not change which profile you are on and it does not alter a
single byte of your vault. Deleting a vault is a separate, explicit operation
with its own confirmation — see Operations.

## The commands

Every account command, with what each one does and does not do, is on
the account command page.

# Benchmarks

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/benchmarks/
Release: 0.0.5
Updated: 2026-08-30

Kaleidoscope is measured on BEAM, a public benchmark for long-term memory in
conversation. The results below are ours: we ran them, on our machines, against
a named alternative. There is no build you can download yet, so you cannot
reproduce them yourself today. Read them with that in mind.

These are **separate experiments**, run on different corpora and different sets
of questions. Each section says which. They answer different questions and are
not steps in one series, so please do not read them as one.

## Twelve times the memories, the same answer quality

*The larger of the two corpora: about seventy-five thousand memories over
thirty-five conversations.*

We grew the store from about six thousand memories to about seventy-five
thousand, spread across thirty-five separate vaults, and ran the questions for
that larger corpus. It scored **0.73** on BEAM's scale, where 1.0 is a perfect
answer to every question — the same score the same configuration reached on the
smaller corpus. Nothing
degraded as the store filled up.

Retrieving a hundred memories for each question instead of fifty changed
nothing either. Past a point, handing the reader more does not help; handing it
the right thing does.

That is the property that matters for memory you mean to keep for years. A store
that answers well when it is empty and badly when it is full is not memory.

## Far better than answering with no memory

*The smaller corpus: twenty conversations. Everything in this section and the
next was measured there, with the same reader and the same judge throughout.*

A model answering with nothing to go on gets most of these questions wrong. With
Kaleidoscope it answers most of them well. This is the largest single difference
in anything we have measured.

Putting the whole conversation into the context window instead does not answer
better than retrieving from memory, and it costs about a hundred and thirty
thousand tokens a question to do it. More context is not the same as the right
context.

## Level with mem0, at a quarter fewer tokens

*Same smaller corpus, same twenty conversations.*

We ran mem0's own system on those conversations, using mem0's own prompt and
mem0's own judge, and compared it with ours. **The answer quality matches.** Ours
gets there on **8,173 prompt tokens a question against mem0's 10,762 — 24%
fewer.**

We are not claiming to beat mem0. On this benchmark the two are level, and the
difference is what it costs to get there. mem0 has never published a BEAM score
of its own; the number above is our measurement of their system, not theirs.

## Writing is fast when you write in batches

At ten thousand memories in a vault, storing a memory takes about **76
milliseconds**.\* That is measured end to end — starting the process, opening
the vault, admitting the memory and refreshing the index — not just the part
inside the engine.

\* Writing twenty at a time. A single write on its own costs far more, because
most of the cost is paid once per call rather than once per memory. Batch your
writes.

## What we have not measured

Everything here comes from one benchmark on one kind of workload: long,
multi-session conversations. We have not measured code repositories, documents,
or anything else you might point memory at.

We also chose the settings we ran by trying them against the very questions we
then scored, without holding a set of questions back, so treat all of this as
our best case rather than a promise. The full method — every arm, every
measurement, and the ones that did not work — will be published alongside the
first release.

---

# Brand assets

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/brand/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Three marks belong to one system, and all of them are generated from a single
geometry table in the `brand/` folder. This page renders every file in that
folder so you can see which drawing a file name refers to, and on which ground
it is meant to sit.

Half of these marks are drawn in ink for paper and half in bone or brass for a
dark ground, so a contact sheet on one background hides half of them. The light
panels below are painted `#EAE7E0` — the value the bone theme calls `raised`,
and the same value this site calls `--k-ink`. One hex, doing both jobs.

## The domain map decides the theme

This is the part that gets applied wrong, so it is first. Which brand a surface
wears, and on which stock, is not a taste call:

| domain | brand | stock | theme |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kleosresearch.xyz` | Kleos — the lab, the front door | bone `#F4F2EC` | `kleos-light` |
| `memory.kleosresearch.xyz` | Kaleidoscope — the product | ink `#0B0B0C` | `kaleidoscope-dark` |

Crossing the subdomain crosses the stock. The subdomain is the tagline:
`memory.` says what the product does before the page loads. This site is the
second row, which is why every panel on it is ink and why brass appears here
and nowhere else.

## Where these files come from

The `brand/` folder holds one generator, `build.py`, and four geometry tables.
Running it writes all 40 SVGs and, with `--png`, all 26 rasters:

```bash
python3 brand/build.py --png
```

Every generated file opens with the line
`Kleos brand system — generated by brand/build.py. Do not hand-edit.` Take that
literally. To change a mark, change the table and run the generator again;
editing an SVG by hand produces a file that the next run silently reverts, and
in the meantime the copy you edited disagrees with every other size of the same
drawing.

Four files in `brand/` are hand-maintained rather than generated: the README,
the generator, and the two token exports. The tokens are republished here as
kleos-brand.css.

Copies of these marks exist in other repositories. `brand/` is the only source;
a copy that disagrees with it is wrong, and the fix is always to re-copy rather
than to redraw.

## Colour

Six values per theme, and the only difference between the two themes is that
brass takes a darker cut on bone so it clears contrast. Same hue, not a second
colour.

### kaleidoscope-dark

The product, on ink. These six are the palette this site is painted in.

  bg#0B0B0C
  raised#131315
  rule#232325
  muted#8C887F
  ink#EAE7E0
  brass#CFA757

### kleos-light

The lab, on paper. Nothing on this site is painted in these; they are here
because the marks below are drawn for them.

  bg#F4F2EC
  raised#EAE7E0
  rule#D8D4C9
  muted#6A675F
  ink#141310
  brass#8A6A22

### Fixed

Constant across both stocks. Do not re-theme them.

  icon-tile#0E0D0C
  copilot-tile#17161C
  copilot-sky#5FB2EC
  copilot-sky-hi#9BD4FF
  copilot-sky-lo#4593D8
  copilot-sky-text#2F79B5

The last one is a text token. Sky at `#5FB2EC` fails contrast as type on paper,
so links there take `#2F79B5` instead. It is never used to fill an icon.

## Kleos — the ledger line

Two full-width rules with the record between them. This is the house mark: the
lab, the organisation, and the endorsement line "a kleos project" at the foot of
this page.

The bars thicken and lengthen as the mark shrinks, so the three elements stay
separable. Pick the cut by the tile you are drawing into, never by scaling one
file. Every cut ships three ways: `currentColor` for inline HTML, and two
hardcoded variants for contexts that cannot inherit a colour.

| tile | bars | inherits | on bone | on ink |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 48px and up | 48×7 | `kleos-mark.svg` | `kleos-mark-ink.svg` | `kleos-mark-bone.svg` |
| 40 and 64 | 52×9 | `kleos-mark-40.svg` | `kleos-mark-40-ink.svg` | `kleos-mark-40-bone.svg` |
| 32 | 54×10 | `kleos-mark-32.svg` | `kleos-mark-32-ink.svg` | `kleos-mark-32-bone.svg` |
| 16 | 56×12 | `kleos-mark-16.svg` | `kleos-mark-16-ink.svg` | `kleos-mark-16-bone.svg` |

Kleos never drops its centre square, at any size. Only the Kaleidoscope
app-icon ladder does that.

### On bone

All five rendered at 56px, so the cuts can be compared. In use they would be
16, 32, 40 and 48-and-up.

    kleos/kleos-mark.svg
    currentColor · any stock, inline only

    kleos/kleos-mark-ink.svg
    ink #141310 · base cut, on bone

    kleos/kleos-mark-40-ink.svg
    ink · the 40 and 64 tiles

    kleos/kleos-mark-32-ink.svg
    ink · the 32 tile

    kleos/kleos-mark-16-ink.svg
    ink · the 16 tile, fattest bars

The first cell is the `currentColor` file. Loaded through an `img` element it
cannot inherit anything and falls back to black, which is why the hardcoded
variants exist at all. Inline the file in your markup and it takes the colour
of its parent.

### On ink

    kleos/kleos-mark-bone.svg
    bone #EAE7E0 · the endorsement cut

    kleos/kleos-mark-40-bone.svg
    bone · the 40 and 64 tiles

    kleos/kleos-mark-32-bone.svg
    bone · the 32 tile

    kleos/kleos-mark-16-bone.svg
    bone · the 16 tile

### Avatars and favicons

Kleos is ink on bone, and that is the identity rather than an exception: a
tiled mark reads against light browser chrome and dark browser chrome alike,
which a bare transparent mark does not. Each tile below is rendered at its own
size.

The hairline ring is inset, not outset. An icon canvas has no outside, and at
16px that one pixel is the entire margin — the ring closes on the bars and the
mark turns to mush. So 16 ships without a ring; 32 and up keep it.

    kleos/avatar-16.svg
    16 · no ring, by design

    kleos/avatar-32.svg
    32 · inset hairline #C3BEB1

    kleos/avatar-40.svg
    40 · circular, the org avatar

    kleos/avatar-64.svg
    64 · square, ringed

    kleos/avatar-180.svg
    180 · apple-touch: square, unringed, because iOS applies its own mask

    kleos/favicon.svg
    byte-identical to avatar-32 · one file has to serve 16 and 32

The 40 is the only circular tile in the system.

## Kaleidoscope — the same atom, rotated

One bar swept four times about the centre with a falling opacity cascade, plus
the centre square the Kleos mark also has. That shared square is the entire
relationship between parent and product.

Two rules govern this mark and neither is negotiable. The cascade is the mark:
flatten the four bars to one opacity and it reads as a static frame rather than
a rotation, which is a different logo. And the centre is a square, never a
circle — a circle severs the link to Kleos.

| tile | bars | centre | inherits | on ink | on bone |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| display | 28×7 | yes | `kaleidoscope-mark.svg` | `kaleidoscope-mark-brass.svg` | `kaleidoscope-mark-brass-on-bone.svg` |
| 64 | 28×8 | yes | `kaleidoscope-mark-64.svg` | `kaleidoscope-mark-64-brass.svg` | `kaleidoscope-mark-64-brass-on-bone.svg` |
| 32 | 30×10 | dropped | `kaleidoscope-mark-32.svg` | `kaleidoscope-mark-32-brass.svg` | `kaleidoscope-mark-32-brass-on-bone.svg` |
| 16 | 32×12 | dropped | `kaleidoscope-mark-16.svg` | `kaleidoscope-mark-16-brass.svg` | `kaleidoscope-mark-16-brass-on-bone.svg` |

Read that ladder as what it is: the macOS app-icon ladder, where the art sits
inside a squircle at those pixel sizes. Below 32 the centre square fills in and
muddies, so it comes out — but only there. For an inline mark in running
interface work, a header, a footer, a lockup, use the display cut with its
centre square even at 20px. The mark in this site's header is that cut at 18px.

### On ink

    kaleidoscope-mark-brass.svg
    brass #CFA757 · display cut, centre square

    kaleidoscope-mark-64-brass.svg
    brass · 64 tile, centre square

    kaleidoscope-mark-32-brass.svg
    brass · 32 tile, no centre

    kaleidoscope-mark-16-brass.svg
    brass · 16 tile, bars reach the edge

### On bone

Brass darkens to `#8A6A22` on paper. It is the same hue pulled down until it
clears contrast, not a second brand colour, and it appears on no surface this
site paints.

    kaleidoscope-mark.svg
    currentColor · the inline file, black through an img

    kaleidoscope-mark-brass-on-bone.svg
    brass #8A6A22 · display cut

    kaleidoscope-mark-64-brass-on-bone.svg
    64 tile, centre square

    kaleidoscope-mark-32-brass-on-bone.svg
    32 tile, no centre

    kaleidoscope-mark-16-brass-on-bone.svg
    16 tile, no centre

### App icons and favicon

Brass on its own dark tile, which is the inverse of the Kleos treatment and
gets to the same place: the icon reads against light or dark browser chrome
because it brings its own ground. Shown here on bone so the edge of that tile
is visible. The squircle sits at 824/1024 of the canvas, with the art inset a
further step inside it.

The squircle is the only rounded thing in the system. Marks are always
sharp-cornered.

    kaleidoscope/app-icon-16.svg
    16 · three blades of cascade, no centre

    kaleidoscope/app-icon-32.svg
    32 · no centre square

    kaleidoscope/app-icon-64.svg
    64 · last size that keeps the centre

    kaleidoscope/app-icon-128.svg
    128 · its own cut, not the 1024 scaled

    kaleidoscope/app-icon-1024.svg
    the master · shown at 180 · every raster comes from here

    kaleidoscope/favicon.svg
    byte-identical to app-icon-32 · this is /favicon.svg here

## 0xCopilot — the turbine

The one fixed point in the system. A blade rotated six times, filled with a sky
gradient from `#9BD4FF` to `#4593D8`, over a dark hub and a sky dot, on the
`#17161C` tile at every size. Never recoloured for a surface, never inverted
onto paper, never given a light-mode variant. The stock around it varies; the
icon does not.

Its small-size simplification is the one Kaleidoscope makes with its centre
square: at 16 the blade count drops from six to three, because six will not
survive.

The first three files carry no tile of their own. They are transparent, and the
consumer has to place them on `#17161C`, which is what the panels below do.

    0xcopilot/turbine-mark.svg
    base · six blades, hub #0D0C10, dot #5FB2EC

    0xcopilot/turbine-mark-32.svg
    32 · thicker blades, larger hub

    0xcopilot/turbine-mark-16.svg
    16 · three blades, not six

    0xcopilot/app-icon.svg
    the only 0xCopilot file that ships its own tile

Each of the four uses a different gradient identifier, so several can be
inlined on one page without colliding.

## Rasters

Twenty-six PNGs, written by the same run with `--png`. Use them where an SVG
cannot go: an operating system icon slot, an email, a store listing.

        Family
        Sizes
        Rasterised from

        kaleidoscope-app-icon
        1024, 512, 256, 128, 64, 32, 16
        app-icon-1024.svg

        kaleidoscope-favicon
        180, 32, 16
        kaleidoscope/favicon.svg

        kaleidoscope-mark-brass
        1024, 256, 64
        kaleidoscope-mark-brass.svg, transparent

        kleos-favicon
        180, 32, 16
        avatar-180, avatar-32, avatar-16 — each its own cut

        kleos-avatar
        400
        avatar-40.svg, the circular cut

        kleos-mark-ink
        1024, 256, 64
        kleos-mark-ink.svg, transparent

        kleos-mark-bone
        1024, 256, 64
        kleos-mark-bone.svg, transparent

        0xcopilot-app-icon
        1024, 256, 64
        0xcopilot/app-icon.svg

Two things in that table are worth knowing before you use it.

The Kleos favicon rasters each come from the tile carrying their own optical
cut, so the 16 is the 16 drawing and not the 180 scaled down. The Kaleidoscope
app-icon rasters do the opposite on purpose: all seven come from the 1024
master, so the 32 and 16 PNGs carry the centre square that the 32 and 16 SVG
cuts drop. If you need the optical cut at those sizes, take the SVG.

## Not cut here

No wordmark lockup exists as an asset, and one should not be added. An SVG
carrying live text renders differently wherever the typeface is absent, which
turns the lockup into a trap. Set wordmarks in HTML with the webfont instead:

| wordmark | face | weight | tracking | case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KLEOS | Newsreader | 400 | .055em, .05em below 14px, .06em at 14px | upper |
| Kaleidoscope | Newsreader | 400 | 0 | sentence |

Newsreader is never set bold. Inter carries interface text; JetBrains Mono
carries metadata, uppercase and tracked. 0xCopilot runs its own stack — Space
Grotesk for display, Instrument Sans for body, the same mono.

There is also no `.ico` in `brand/`. The generator writes SVG and PNG only, so
the `favicon.ico` this site serves was assembled by hand around canonical
pixels and nothing regenerates it when a mark changes. Treat it as the one file
here that can go quietly stale.

## What the source folder does not cover

Worth stating so nobody fills the gap by redrawing something.

The 0xCopilot set is the thinnest. It has no macOS-grid app icon of the kind
Kaleidoscope has — one tile inset at 824/1024 rather than filling the canvas —
and its raster ladder stops at 1024, 256 and 64, with no favicon or
apple-touch rungs. Surfaces that need those sizes have been cutting their own,
which is how a mark ends up with two versions of its corner radius. The fix
belongs in the geometry table, not in the surface.

The README in `brand/` still carries a warning that this domain ships the wrong
mark, no favicon and a half-wired theme. That was true when it was written and
is not true now: the header mark here is the canonical display cut, the four
icon links and the theme colour are wired, and the whole palette resolves. The
mark on every page of this site is checked geometrically at build time — bar
count, rotation angles, the opacity cascade, the centre square, and the absence
of any rounded corner — so it cannot drift back without the build refusing.

---

# CLI reference

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/
Updated: 2026-08-30

`kscope` is the command. It creates a vault, wires your editor to it, and
answers questions about both.

```bash
npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope
kscope --help
```

The full help text is the authority on every
argument.

## The verbs

| To do this | Run | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Create a vault and wire your editor | `init` | Connect an editor |
| Write the instruction file and skill | `init` | Agent instructions |
| Name a vault so an editor can start with it | `init-profile`, `profile create`, `profile import` | Profiles and vaults |
| See, inspect or forget a profile | `profile list`, `profile show`, `profile launch`, `profile remove` | Profiles and vaults |
| Find out which vault you are talking to | `where` | Diagnostics |
| Check the key, the model, the vault | `gate`, `activate`, `model`, `vault-verify` | Diagnostics |
| Run an engine for an agent | `mcp`, `serve`, `context`, `call` | MCP reference |
| Migrate, preview or delete a vault | `vault-migrate`, `vault-preview`, `vault-delete` | Operations |
| Read the tool contract | `schema` | MCP reference |
| Read the third-party notices | `licences` | — |

`kscope init` appears twice because one run does both jobs: it creates the
vault, then tells every agent on this machine that the vault exists.

## The flags

| Flag | On | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `--profile NAME` | `mcp`, `serve`, `context`, `call` | Work in the vault that profile names. Nothing else accepts it. |
| `--no-wire` | `init` | Create the vault and write no editor configuration. Real, though `--help` does not list it. |
| `--root-only` | `where` | Print only the vault root and the project it came from. |
| `--cross-backend` | `vault-verify` | Widen the check. |
| `--help`, `-h` | any invocation | Print the command surface. |
| `--version`, `-V` | any invocation | Print the version. |

`kscope init` takes no `--profile`. It works on the directory you are in, or on
a root you name as a positional argument.

There is no `--engine`, no `--dry-run` and no `--yes`. An unknown verb prints
the help text; an unknown argument to `init` is refused by name, and nothing is
created.

## Where the wiring goes

| What | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| MCP server entry | your home directory | An agent runs your work in a worktree or a temporary clone, and an entry inside one project directory is never read from there. |
| Instruction file and skill | the project | Git carries them into that worktree or clone. |

## What init writes, and what it leaves alone

- Kaleidoscope writes only the block it owns, between ownership comments
  wherever the file format has room for them.
- Every file it writes gets a receipt beside it:
  `config.toml.kaleidoscope-owner.json` beside a host configuration,
  `CLAUDE.md.kaleidoscope-instruction-owner.json` beside an instruction file.
- A file it changes rather than creates is copied to
  `.kaleidoscope-backup` first. The rest of the file is untouched.
- If what it finds no longer matches the receipt, it stops at that file and
  reports that step as failed. The other steps still run.
- The configuration it writes carries no token, no provider key and no vault
  location. It names this executable, a profile, and the tools `search` and
  `remember`.
- Running `kscope init` again is safe. An existing vault is left as it is and
  the wiring is re-checked.

## The second executable

Some verbs written about elsewhere — `connect`, `disconnect`, `config`,
`doctor`, `teardown`, `profile use`, `instructions install`, and the whole
account surface — belong to `kaleidoscope`, a second executable built from
source and published on no channel. Nothing on this site asks you to run one.
Account commands lists them.

---

# Account commands

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/account/
Updated: 2026-08-30

None of the commands on this page runs today. They belong to `kaleidoscope`, a
second executable built from source and published on no channel, and the account
service they would reach answers `provider not configured`. They are written
down so you can see the shape of signing in before it arrives.

`kscope`, the command you have, carries no account commands at all.

## What there is instead

The alpha is opened by a key, not by an account. Email
contact@kleosresearch.xyz for one, then:

```bash
kscope activate
```

`activate` takes the key as an argument, from `KALEIDOSCOPE_API_KEY`, from the
key file, or from standard input. It stores the key at the path `kscope gate`
prints, so an engine your editor starts with an empty environment still finds
it, and it waits for the verdict rather than leaving the next command to
discover an empty cache.

You do not need an account to use Kaleidoscope. Your memory lives on your
machine and has never needed one.

## Sign in and out

```bash
kaleidoscope login
kaleidoscope login --device
kaleidoscope status --json
kaleidoscope logout
kaleidoscope logout --all-devices
kaleidoscope logout --local-only
```

| Command | What it would do |
|---|---|
| `login` | Ordinary browser sign-in. |
| `login --device` | Code-based sign-in, for a machine with no browser. |
| `status --json` | Report your account session on this machine. Unrelated to the status page, which is about what is available. |
| `logout` | Remove the credential here and revoke it. |
| `logout --all-devices` | End every session on the account. |
| `logout --local-only` | Remove the local credential and warn you that nothing was revoked remotely. |

No form of `logout` changes which profile a command resolves to, or a byte of
your vault.

## Linked sign-in providers

```bash
kaleidoscope account link PROVIDER
kaleidoscope account identities
kaleidoscope account unlink EXTERNAL_IDENTITY_UUID
kaleidoscope account revoke-session
```

| Command | What it would do |
|---|---|
| `account link PROVIDER` | Attach a sign-in provider to the account. |
| `account identities` | List the opaque IDs, which is where `unlink` gets its argument. |
| `account unlink UUID` | Detach one of them. |
| `account revoke-session` | Revoke the session you are using. It does not deactivate an account. |

## Devices

```bash
kaleidoscope devices list
kaleidoscope devices revoke DEVICE_UUID
```

The devices attached to your account, and how to detach one. Revoking a device
is an account operation; the vault on that device is untouched.

## Local account reference

```bash
kaleidoscope profile account show
kaleidoscope profile account bind ACCOUNT_UUID
kaleidoscope profile account unbind
```

These three write a non-secret account ID into a local profile and nothing more:
no engine started, no service contacted, no vault touched, no credential stored.
Each takes an optional profile name and defaults to the one you are in.

## The boundary

Account traffic goes to a closed list of account-only routes and never touches
the memory engine. A guard rejects memory fields, profile fields and absolute
local paths before anything is sent.

Account and devices covers what signing in would mean and
where a credential would be kept.

---

# Connect an editor or agent

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/connect/
Updated: 2026-08-30

`kscope init` creates the project's memory and writes the entry your editor
needs to find it. Run both commands:

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
kscope profile import default ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
```

The entry `init` writes starts the engine with `--profile default`, and creating
the vault does not create that profile. The second command writes it. Skip it
and your editor shows `profile does not exist` and nothing else.

Restart your editor. Until you do it is still running with the configuration it
started with.

## What you should see

```
kscope: created vault ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope (repository default)
kscope: wrote /.kaleidoscope/ to a new ~/your-project/.gitignore
kscope: wired codex, claude-code, cursor, opencode
kscope:   register the MCP server with codex
kscope:   agents for codex
kscope:   skill for codex
...
kscope: restart your agent, then ask it to search your memory.
```

One line per step, and a named failure for any step that could not be written.
`init` wires an agent only when that agent's configuration directory already
exists on this machine. If it finds none it writes an `AGENTS.md`, which most
other agents read, and says so.

## What lands where

| Agent | MCP entry | Instructions | Skill |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `~/.claude.json` | a marked block in `CLAUDE.md` | `.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml` | a marked block in `AGENTS.md` | `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc` | none |
| OpenCode | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` | a marked block in `AGENTS.md` | `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` |

MCP entries go in your home directory; instructions and skills go in the
project, where git carries them into the worktree or clone your agent works in.

Each file gets a receipt beside it — `.kaleidoscope-owner.json` for a host
configuration, `.kaleidoscope-instruction-owner.json` for an instruction file or
skill. A file that already existed is copied to `.kaleidoscope-backup`
first.

Nothing written carries a vault path, a provider key or an account credential.
The entry names this executable, a profile, and the two tools `search` and
`remember`.

## Running it again

`kscope init` again is safe. A root that is already a vault is reported and left
exactly as it is; the wiring is re-checked and repaired.

If a Kaleidoscope block no longer matches its receipt — you edited inside the
markers, or wrote an entry by hand — that step stops and names the file. The
other steps still run.

To create the vault and write no editor configuration at all:

```bash
kscope init --no-wire
```

## Removing it

There is no `disconnect` verb on `kscope`, so remove the wiring by hand. Delete
each of these with the receipt beside it:

- the `kaleidoscope` entry under `mcpServers` in `~/.claude.json`,
  `~/.cursor/mcp.json` and `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`
- the block between the `kaleidoscope-manager` markers in `~/.codex/config.toml`
- the marked block in `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`
- `.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/`, `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` and
  `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc`

`npm uninstall -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope` removes the command itself.

None of that touches your memory. An entry pointing at a vault that no longer
exists is harmless, and `kscope init` writes the wiring back.
Operations covers moving, backing up and deleting a vault.

---

# Diagnostics

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/diagnostics/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Four commands answer the four questions that come up when something looks
wrong. None of them reads or changes a memory.

| Question | Command | Healthy answer |
|---|---|---|
| Which vault is this? | `kscope where` | the root you expected |
| Is my key working? | `kscope gate` | `"status":"enforcing"` and a key file path |
| Is the engine complete? | `kscope model` | `"status":"bundled"` |
| Is the vault intact? | `kscope vault-verify ROOT` | `"status":"complete"` |

## Which vault is this?

```bash
kscope where
```

Prints the vault this directory resolves to, the workspace, principal and
journal inside it, and where each of those came from. Run it when you are not
sure which project's memory your agent is talking to.

`--root-only` narrows the output to the root and the project it was resolved
from.

## Is my key working?

```bash
kscope gate
```

Reports whether this build enforces the licence check, which commands the check
refuses, and the directory it reads the key from. It reads no key and makes no
authorization decision, so it answers even on a binary that is refusing
everything else.

```bash
kscope activate
```

Installs a key and waits for the verdict. It takes the key as an argument, from
`KALEIDOSCOPE_API_KEY`, from the key file, or from standard input.
`"entitled":true` means you are set up.

| | Commands |
|---|---|
| Need a key | `mcp`, `serve`, `context`, `call` |
| Work without one | `where`, `schema`, `model`, `gate`, `vault-preview`, `vault-verify`, `vault-migrate` |

## Is the engine complete?

```bash
kscope model
```

Prints the semantic embedding model this build carries, its dimensions, and the
SHA-256 of its two files. Anything but `"status":"bundled"` means search gets
quietly worse rather than failing, so check it directly.

## Is the vault intact?

```bash
kscope vault-verify ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
```

Counts what is stored and reports whether the copies agree. It reads only. Add
`--cross-backend` to widen the check.

For the full report, `call doctor` reads one JSON request from standard input
and returns JSON. `inspect` is the mode that only looks:

```bash
echo '{"mode":"inspect"}' | kscope call doctor
```

`call` needs a key. It is an operator command, so your agent is never offered
it.

---

# Agent instructions

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/instructions/
Updated: 2026-08-30

An agent uses memory only if something told it to. `kscope init` writes two
things into your project for that: a marked block in the instruction file your
agent already reads, and the skill itself.

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
```

There is no separate command and no flag to remember. The steps go past as it
works — `claude for claude-code`, `skill for claude-code`, `agents for codex` —
one line each, and a named failure for any that could not be written.

## Where each agent reads them

| Agent | Instruction file | Skill |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | a marked block in `CLAUDE.md` | `.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` |
| Codex | a marked block in `AGENTS.md` | `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` |
| OpenCode | a marked block in `AGENTS.md` | `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` |
| Cursor | `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc`, the whole file | none: Cursor reads no skill directory |
| none detected | a marked block in `AGENTS.md` | none |

The skill directory differs per agent, and a skill written to the wrong one is a
file the agent never loads. `kscope init` writes the path the agent in front of
it reads.

All of it goes into the project, none into your home directory. Git is what
carries these files into the worktree or clone your agent works in.

Give your agent the skill has both files for download if you
would rather install one yourself.

## The markers

Everything appended to an existing file sits between two ownership comments, and
every file Kaleidoscope owns outright gets a
`.kaleidoscope-instruction-owner.json` receipt beside it.

That pair is read before the file is touched. It is what makes a second
`kscope init` update the block instead of duplicating it, and what makes an
exact removal possible.

Edit the text between the markers and that one step stops and hands the file
back rather than overwriting your work. The remaining steps still run.

## Installing or removing one on its own

Not on `kscope`. Installing is what `kscope init` does; removing is by hand, and
connect an editor or agent lists the files to
delete.

---

# Profiles and vaults

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/profiles/
Updated: 2026-08-30

A vault is one memory store: a directory at a path you chose. A profile is a
name for one — an absolute root, the three identifiers inside it, and the
durability. An editor or agent is started with a profile name; nothing else is.

## Create a vault

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
```

`init` resolves the root, creates the vault there, and prints the path along
with where the path came from. Resolution order:

| Order | Root |
|---|---|
| 1 | `KSCOPE_ROOT` |
| 2 | `.kaleidoscope/` under the repository's main checkout |
| 3 | `.kaleidoscope/` under the working directory |

A root that is already a vault is reported and left exactly as it is. Add
`--no-wire` to create the vault and touch no editor configuration.

To control the moment a vault records as its creation, name the root and an
RFC 3339 instant. This form creates the vault and wires nothing:

```bash
kscope init /absolute/path/to/vault 2026-08-30T09:00:00Z
```

Durability is the last word on either form. `process-local` is the default and
the only value any release accepts, so `kscope init durable-local` is refused
before anything is written. What `process-local` promises is that a vault stays
complete-or-absent across a process crash or a hard kill.

## Name a vault

```bash
kscope profile import default ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
```

| Command | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `profile import NAME ROOT` | The vault exists. Reads its identity and writes the profile. This is the one to run after `kscope init`. |
| `init-profile NAME ROOT CREATED_AT` | You want the vault and the profile in one step. |
| `profile create NAME ROOT WORKSPACE_ID PRINCIPAL_ID JOURNAL` | You already hold the identifiers. They are verified against the vault. |

`default` is the profile the wiring starts your agent with, and `kscope init`
does not create it. Until it exists, anything started with `--profile default`
refuses with `profile does not exist`.

If `init-profile` commits the vault and then fails to write the profile, it
keeps the vault and prints the `kscope profile import` command that finishes the
job.

None of the three creates or relocates vault data, and none stores a secret. A
profile is a pointer.

## List, inspect, remove

```bash
kscope profile list
kscope profile show default
kscope profile launch default
kscope profile remove work
```

| Command | Prints |
|---|---|
| `profile list` | Every profile on this machine, each validated against its vault as it is read. |
| `profile show NAME` | One profile: root, workspace, principal, journal, durability. |
| `profile launch NAME` | The launch descriptor an editor entry is made of — this executable's absolute path, `mcp --profile NAME`, and the tools `search` and `remember`. No vault coordinates, no key. |
| `profile remove NAME` | The removal. The vault the profile pointed at stays on your disk. |

Deleting a profile, naming a different one, or reinstalling Kaleidoscope leaves
every byte of every vault where it was. Getting rid of the memory itself is a
separate act; see Operations.

## When no profile is named

There is no active profile and no `kscope profile use`. `mcp`, `serve`,
`context` and `call` resolve a vault by the same three rules `init` uses. Print
the address they will arrive at before you rely on it:

```bash
kscope where
```

A resolved root that is not a vault is refused by all four, naming the path and
where the path came from. They never create one.

## Binding a profile to an account

`profile account show`, `bind` and `unbind` are not on this executable. The only
account-shaped command that ships is `kscope activate`, which stores your key;
the rest is on the account page.

---

# Platforms

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/compatibility/
Updated: 2026-08-30

`npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope` brings down the package built for
your machine. You need a key to run it, and nothing is signed for release.

## Built and published

        Platform
        Architecture
        On npm
        Run by us

Install and run any of them. We have run it by hand on one machine, and the
status page says what that covered.

## Compiler checks

A compiler check is not a build: nothing was assembled, linked or run. Three of
the platforms below were built and published afterwards, and appear in the table
above.

        Platform
        Architecture
        Compiler check

The check covers the memory engine's source only, not the client libraries, and
it was run from .

## Windows

Windows is not supported yet.

| | |
|---|---|
| Package | not published |
| Creating a vault | refused on purpose |
| What is missing | file locking, link handling, and flushing writes to the disk |

Until that filesystem work lands, `kscope` stops rather than writing memory it
cannot stand behind.

The same matrix, machine-readable:
platform-support.json.

# Concepts

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/concepts/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Five words carry most of these pages.

| term | what it is |
|---|---|
| vault | The `.kaleidoscope` folder holding your memories, the graph, and the exposure ledger. One per project, on your disk. |
| profile | A named pointer to one vault. Editors are registered against `default`. |
| engine | The native program that stores, ranks and serves memory, and speaks MCP over stdio. |
| manager | The setup half — creating a vault, editing editor configuration, installing agent guidance. Compiled into `kscope`. |
| account | A product account a device could be bound to. Not something you can create today. |

## Where your memory lives

Your memories are files in the vault, on the machine that wrote them. Nothing is
uploaded, and there is no service behind the engine to upload to.

Deleting `.kaleidoscope` deletes that project's memory and nothing else.
Operations covers moving, inspecting and verifying a vault.

## One vault, every agent

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, the framework SDKs and any generic MCP
client read the same profile. They see the same memories because they resolve
the same vault.

Each editor stores its MCP configuration in a different format. `kscope init`
writes each one and starts every server the same way:

```bash
kscope mcp --profile default
```

Which vault a command resolves to, when it names no profile, comes from the
project directory:

```bash
kscope where
```

## What ships

You install one npm package, `@kleos-research/kaleidoscope`. It pulls in a
second package built for your platform.

| package | carries |
|---|---|
| `@kleos-research/kaleidoscope` | the `kscope` command, the client, and the resolver that finds the platform payload |
| the platform package | the engine, as object code, with the manager's setup half compiled in |

Neither contains engine source, and neither downloads anything at install time.
Install has the machine requirements.

## What does not ship yet

Signing in, binding a profile to an account, and listing or revoking devices
belong to a second executable named `kaleidoscope`, published on no channel.
Pages that show its commands mark them as not shipped.

A profile can record one account UUID locally. That changes neither its vault
nor its credentials.

There is no hosted memory service, and no Python package you can use —
`kscope-memory` on PyPI is a 0.0.0 placeholder. See
Privacy for the boundary in full.

---

# Getting started

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/getting-started/
Release: 0.0.5
Updated: 2026-08-30

Four steps, about two minutes. You need macOS or Linux and Node.js 18 or newer.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope
```

You get the `kscope` command and the engine built for your platform.

## 2. Activate your key

```bash
export KALEIDOSCOPE_API_KEY=<your key>
kscope activate
```

Look for `"entitled":true` and a fragment of your key. `activate` stores the
key, so new terminals find it without the `export`.

No key yet? Email
contact@kleosresearch.xyz. To keep the key
out of your shell, write it instead into the `api-key` file at the path
`kscope gate` prints, at mode `600`.

## 3. Give a project a memory

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
kscope profile import default ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
```

Expect output like this:

```
kscope: created vault ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope (repository default)
kscope: wrote /.kaleidoscope/ to a new ~/your-project/.gitignore
kscope: wired codex, claude-code, cursor, opencode
kscope:   register the MCP server with codex
kscope:   agents for codex
...
kscope: restart your agent, then ask it to search your memory.
```

The `wired` line names the editors `init` found on this machine; it skips any
whose configuration directory does not exist. `profile import` names the new
vault `default`, which is the profile the wiring starts each editor with.

To create the vault and write no configuration, run `kscope init --no-wire`.
Connect an editor lists what lands where, per editor.

## 4. Restart your agent, then talk to it

Your agent now has two tools, `search` and `remember`. You never call them
yourself.

Ask it what you decided about a design last week. Tell it you prefer a
particular approach. It picks the tool.

If it does not seem to know its memory is there,
give it the skill — a short file that teaches it when to read
and when to write. Otherwise see
Troubleshooting.

## Removing it

Delete `.kaleidoscope` from a project to delete that project's memory.
`npm uninstall -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope` removes the command and leaves
every vault alone. Operations covers moving and inspecting
a vault.

---

# Editors, agents and frameworks

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Every page here assumes `kscope` is installed and activated —
Getting started covers both.

Everything on this page reaches one engine on your machine and sees the same two
tools, `search` and `remember`.

## Editors

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
kscope profile import default ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
```

Restart the editor, then ask it to search your memory.

`kscope init` wires every editor whose configuration directory already exists.
`kscope init --no-wire` creates the vault and writes no editor configuration.

| Editor | MCP entry | Instructions | Skill |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `~/.claude.json` | `CLAUDE.md` | `.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml` | `AGENTS.md` | `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc` | none |
| OpenCode | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` | `AGENTS.md` | `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` |

Cursor gets a rule file and no skill.

## Everything else

Other MCP clients and agent frameworks read the same launch descriptor.

```bash
kscope profile launch default
```

| Client | Page |
|---|---|
| Any MCP client | Any other MCP client |
| Claude Agent SDK | Claude Agent SDK |
| OpenAI Agents SDK | OpenAI Agents SDK |
| LangChain | LangChain |
| LangGraph | LangGraph |
| CrewAI | CrewAI |

## Before any of it

`npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope` gives you `kscope`, and running it
needs a key. Install covers both steps.
Give your agent the skill is the file that tells an agent when to
read its memory and when to write to it.

# Codex

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/codex/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Install and activate first — Getting started covers both. Without a
key the wiring below succeeds and the server refuses with `E_NO_KEY` the moment your editor
starts it.

`kscope init` wires Codex when `~/.codex` exists.

## Wire it

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
kscope profile import default ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
```

Run both, in that order. Skip the import and Codex reports
`profile does not exist`.

Restart Codex, then ask it to search your memory.

## What init writes

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| MCP entry | `~/.codex/config.toml`, inside a `kaleidoscope-manager` marker block |
| Instructions | `AGENTS.md`, between marker comments |
| Skill | `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` |
| Receipt | `~/.codex/config.toml.kaleidoscope-owner.json`, and a `.kaleidoscope-instruction-owner.json` beside each project file |
| Backup | `~/.codex/config.toml.kaleidoscope-backup`, when the file was already there |

```toml
# >>> kaleidoscope-manager owner=kaleidoscope-manager-v1 host=codex
[mcp_servers.kaleidoscope]
command = "/absolute/path/to/kscope"
args = ["mcp", "--profile", "default"]
enabled = true
required = false
startup_timeout_sec = 10
tool_timeout_sec = 30
enabled_tools = ["search", "remember"]
default_tools_approval_mode = "writes"

[mcp_servers.kaleidoscope.tools.search]
approval_mode = "approve"
# <<< kaleidoscope-manager owner=kaleidoscope-manager-v1
```

`enabled_tools` names the two tools in Codex's own configuration. Skills go to
`.agents/skills/` here, the same path OpenCode reads; Claude Code reads
`.claude/skills/`.

If `~/.codex/config.toml` already holds an `[mcp_servers.kaleidoscope]` table
outside a marker block, that step fails and the file is not changed. Delete the
table by hand and run `kscope init` again.

## Check it

```bash
kscope profile list
kscope profile launch default
```

`launch` prints the command, the arguments and the tool list — `search` and
`remember` — that the table in `~/.codex/config.toml` should match.

## Remove it

Delete each of these, and the receipt beside it:

- the marker block in `~/.codex/config.toml`
- the marked block in `AGENTS.md`
- `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/`

Your memory stays. Connect an editor or agent covers every
editor at once.

# Any other MCP client

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/generic-mcp/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Any standard MCP client runs Kaleidoscope from the descriptor the engine prints.
You do not hand-write the command.

## Get the descriptor

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init --no-wire
kscope profile import default ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
kscope profile launch default
```

`--no-wire` creates the vault and leaves every editor configuration alone. Drop
it to wire Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode as well.

The last command prints this:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "transport": "stdio",
  "command": "/absolute/path/to/kscope",
  "args": ["mcp", "--profile", "default"],
  "tools": ["search", "remember"],
  "environment": {}
}
```

| Field | What to do with it |
|---|---|
| `command`, `args` | the server definition in your own configuration |
| `transport` | stdio, one long-lived process |
| `tools` | the whole model-facing surface; allow exactly these two |
| `environment` | empty — pass no vault path, key or token |

## Wire it in

Put `command` and `args` into your client's server definition. Start the server
once and reuse the session, rather than one process per tool call.

## Check it

Your client's tool list should hold exactly `search` and `remember`. If
`kscope profile launch default` prints `profile does not exist`, run the
`profile import` above.

## Remove it

Delete the server definition from your own configuration. This route writes
nothing else.

---

# OpenCode

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/opencode/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Install and activate first — Getting started covers both. Without a
key the wiring below succeeds and the server refuses with `E_NO_KEY` the moment your editor
starts it.

`kscope init` wires OpenCode when `~/.config/opencode` or `~/.opencode` exists.

## Wire it

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
kscope profile import default ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
```

Run both, in that order. Skip the import and OpenCode reports
`profile does not exist`.

Restart OpenCode, then ask it to search your memory.

## What init writes

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| MCP entry | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` |
| Instructions | `AGENTS.md`, between marker comments |
| Skill | `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` |
| Receipt | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json.kaleidoscope-owner.json`, and a `.kaleidoscope-instruction-owner.json` beside each project file |
| Backup | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json.kaleidoscope-backup`, when the file was already there |

Skills go to `.agents/skills/` here, the same path Codex reads; Claude Code
reads `.claude/skills/`.

## Which shape you get

OpenCode has two configuration shapes. `init` reads yours and follows it.

| Your `opencode.json` | Entry goes to | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| no `mcp.servers` object | `mcp.kaleidoscope` | `type`, `enabled`, `command` |
| has an `mcp.servers` object | `mcp.servers.kaleidoscope` | `type`, `command`, `codemode: false` |

Both carry `"type": "local"` and a `command` array of the engine's absolute path
followed by `mcp`, `--profile`, `default`. `"codemode": false` keeps `search`
and `remember` visible to the model as tools.

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "kaleidoscope": {
      "type": "local",
      "enabled": true,
      "command": ["/absolute/path/to/kscope", "mcp", "--profile", "default"]
    }
  }
}
```

If both shapes are present, or your file conflicts with the shape Kaleidoscope
already owns, that step fails and the file is not changed. There is no flag to
override it.

## Check it

```bash
kscope profile list
kscope profile launch default
```

`launch` prints the command, the arguments and the tool list — `search` and
`remember` — that the entry in `opencode.json` should match.

## Remove it

Delete each of these, and the receipt beside it:

- the `kaleidoscope` entry in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`
- the marked block in `AGENTS.md`
- `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/`

Your memory stays. Connect an editor or agent covers every
editor at once.

# Licenses and product terms

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/legal/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Reviewed drafts — not yet in force.
The product terms below have been reviewed by legal counsel for Kleos Research Private Limited. Apache-2.0 and CC BY 4.0 are authorized license selections and are in force for the material they cover. The engine EULA, privacy notice, security policy, and support policy have been reviewed but have not yet been adopted: they are not in force, are not offers or contracts, and do not describe terms that govern anything today. They will take effect when the company formally adopts them.

The public software, original documentation, and proprietary engine have
deliberately separate license boundaries. Two of them are settled; the rest are
drafts.

## Authorized public licenses

**Apache-2.0 — in force.** Covers the public manager, SDKs, wrappers,
integrations, and skill, and is carried in those source and package
repositories. It does not license the native engine, model weights, trademarks,
or third-party material.

**CC BY 4.0 — in force.** Covers original documentation. Read the
documentation license scope and the
CC BY 4.0 legal code.

## Product terms — review drafts

| document | plain text |
|---|---|
| Proprietary engine EULA | `ENGINE-EULA.txt` |
| Privacy notice | `PRIVACY-NOTICE.txt` |
| Security policy | `SECURITY-POLICY.txt` |
| Support policy | `SUPPORT-POLICY.txt` |

## What is still outstanding

- **External legal review.** No lawyer has read any of these documents. This is
  the gate that keeps every draft above out of force, and it is now the only one
  of its kind: the drafts are complete rather than partial, so what is left is
  review and a decision to adopt, not missing terms.
- **A compliance question inside them.** The drafts identify the contracting
  party by name, company type, place of registration, and contact address, and
  undertake to supply the registered office address and Corporate Identity
  Number to anyone who asks. Two provisions bear on that and the reviewer has to
  decide both. Section 12(3)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the name,
  registered office address and CIN in a company's business letters, billheads,
  letter papers "and in all its notices and other official publications" —
  whether published product terms are an "official publication" is arguable.
  Rule 26(1) of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014, as substituted with
  effect from 27 July 2016, is the more direct one: it requires a company with a
  website to publish its name, registered office address, CIN, telephone number,
  email and a contact for queries or grievances **on the landing or home page**.
  Both values are already public on the MCA portal against the company name, so
  the question is compliance form rather than confidentiality.
- **Third-party notices.** The embedding model inside the engine is Kleos
  Research's own work and carries no third-party attribution. The open-source
  libraries linked into the engine are a separate question, and they are not yet
  enumerated in the EULA or in the engine's own output. That has to be finished
  before a release.
- **Commitments.** Support scope is deliberately best effort with no response
  time, and no service level exists. That is a decision, not a gap.

# MCP reference

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/mcp/
Release: 0.0.5
Updated: 2026-08-30

Kaleidoscope publishes two MCP tools. `search` reads memory, `remember` writes
it. Nothing else is callable by a model.

`kscope init` registers the server with every editor it finds. Each one starts
`kscope mcp --profile default` and talks to it over stdio at MCP protocol
revision `2025-11-25`.

Machine-readable tool reference ·
Install

## search

Send exactly one of `query` or `memory_id`. Every other field applies to a
ranked `query` and is refused alongside `memory_id`.

| field | notes |
|---|---|
| `query` | Ranked selection. Hits come back under `selected_hits`. |
| `memory_id` | Addressed read of one `mem_...` record. No ranking, no filtering. |
| `top_k` | Memories served, in rank order. Five is a normal value. |
| `candidate_pool` | How many results each retrieval channel may propose before the final cut. Independent of `top_k`. |
| `maximum_context_bytes` | The byte budget the served set is bounded to. |
| `ledger` | Only `true` is accepted. |
| `as_of` | RFC 3339 instant validity is evaluated at. Omitted means now. |
| `scope` | `project`, `branch`, `artifact`. An omitted axis matches every memory. |
| `channels` | Restrict which retrieval channels contribute. |

```json
{"query": "how do we handle database migrations", "top_k": 5}
```

Omit a knob and you get its published default. A value above its ceiling is
refused rather than clamped.

A ranked query writes an exposure row into your vault, recording what it
returned. That is why `ledger: false` is refused: to measure a search without
writing, clone the vault first.

## remember

| field | when | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `mode` | always | `create`, `update`, or `delete`. |
| `content_md` | create, update | The memory as you want to read it back. Must begin with `# `. |
| `semantic_delta` | create, update | The structure committed with it. Fields below. |
| `memory_id` | update, delete | Which memory. |
| `expected_version_id` | update, delete | The active version you are allowed to replace. |
| `items` | instead of the pair above | Up to 20 creates in one call, applied in order. |

Inside `semantic_delta`:

| key | notes |
|---|---|
| `title` | Required. Your words — nothing scrapes it out of `content_md`. |
| `memory_type` | Required. Reuse an accepted name; types are append-only. |
| `facts` | Required, at least one. Each is `subject`, `predicate`, `object`; predicates are snake_case. |
| `entities` | Every surface your facts name, each with `n`, `kind` and `is`. Declare all of them or none. |
| `occurred_at` | When the facts are about, as ``. Kaleidoscope parses no date out of prose. |
| `scope` | `project`, `branch`, `artifact`. |
| `evidence`, `corrections`, `propose`, `temporal`, `context` | Optional. |

```json
{
  "mode": "create",
  "content_md": "# Ana owns the billing service\n\nAna took it over after the payments team split.",
  "semantic_delta": {
    "memory_type": "decision",
    "title": "Ana owns the billing service",
    "entities": [
      {"n": "Ana", "kind": "person", "is": "backend engineer on my team"},
      {"n": "billing service", "kind": "service", "is": "the service that issues invoices"}
    ],
    "facts": [{"subject": "Ana", "predicate": "owns", "object": "billing service"}]
  }
}
```

Write the `is` gloss properly. It is what the engine matches on when it decides
whether two mentions of a name are the same thing, so
`Ana | person | backend engineer on my team` finds far more than `Ana` alone.

`remember` infers nothing. The entities, facts and dates it stores are the ones
you state.

A refusal names the field and what to change it to. Fix it and resend.

## Reading the full contract

The tool schema your host discovered is the authority for the values a build
accepts. Print the same contract from the shell:

```bash
kscope schema remember
kscope schema
```

## What a model never sees

Feedback, lifecycle and import, maintenance, ontology and diagnostics are
operator commands. They are absent from the tool list an agent discovers, and
search results carry no handle that would reach them.

## Next

Discovering the two tools is not the same as using them well.
Give your agent the skill.

---

# Operations

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/operations/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Your memory is one directory: `.kaleidoscope`, inside your project. Everything
on this page works on that directory, and none of it needs an account.

To find out which vault a project resolves to, run `kscope where` — see
Diagnostics.

## Back it up

Close the editors and agents using the vault, then copy the directory whole.

```bash
cp -a ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope ~/backups/your-project-vault
```

A partial copy is not a vault.

## Move it to another machine

Put the directory where you want it, then name it and check it.

```bash
kscope profile import restored ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
kscope vault-verify ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
```

`profile import` reads the identity out of the vault and writes a profile called
`restored`. Start an agent against it with `--profile restored`. `vault-verify`
prints `"status":"complete"` when the copy is whole.

Do not run `kscope init` on a vault you moved. It leaves the vault alone, but it
rewrites that project's editor wiring.

## Delete a vault

Two commands. Preview first.

```bash
kscope vault-preview ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
```

You get an inventory — entries, bytes, what is canonical and what is rebuildable
— and a `confirmation_token`. Pass that token back:

```bash
echo '{"confirmation_token":"TOKEN"}' | kscope vault-delete ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
```

The token belongs to the root you previewed. Point it at another vault and you
get `confirmation token does not match this vault root and path`, and nothing is
deleted.

Deleting the vault deletes the memories in it. `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, the
Cursor rule and the skill directories stay where they are; remove those
separately.

## Update, pin, or roll back

| What you want | Command |
|---|---|
| the current release | `npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope` |
| a version you name | `npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope@` |
| the version you had before | the same command, naming the older version |

Release notes list what is current.

## Remove Kaleidoscope

Four separate things. Removing any of them leaves your memory where it is.

| What | How |
|---|---|
| the package | `npm uninstall -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope` |
| an editor's connection | delete the Kaleidoscope entry from that editor's configuration file |
| the agent instructions | delete the marked block from `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, then `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc` and the `use-kaleidoscope` skill directories |
| the vault | preview and delete it, above |

Every block `kscope init` writes sits between `kaleidoscope-manager` markers,
with a receipt file beside it. Removal is by hand: `kscope` has no disconnect
verb.

## Encrypted vaults on macOS

A vault can live inside an encrypted disk image. This is a frozen macOS preview.

macOS generates the password, keeps it in your login Keychain, and shows you a
recovery key once. Write the recovery key down. It is the only copy.

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| create one | `kscope vault-create  ` |
| open, close | `kscope vault-open`, `kscope vault-close` |
| recover with the key | `kscope vault-recover` |
| move the device package | `kscope vault-export-device`, `kscope vault-import-device` |
| inventory, delete | `kscope vault-encrypted-preview`, `kscope vault-encrypted-delete` |

Each takes a repository path. The help text has the
arguments.

# Install

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/packages/
Release: 0.0.5
Updated: 2026-08-30

```bash
npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope
```

That is the whole install. You need a key to run it — email
contact@kleosresearch.xyz and we will send
you one.

## What your machine needs

| | |
|---|---|
| Operating system | macOS or Linux |
| Architecture | arm64 (Apple Silicon) or x86_64 |
| Node.js | 18 or newer |

Windows is not supported yet. Platforms has the full
matrix.

## What lands on your disk

Two packages, both at version 0.0.5.

| Package | Carries |
|---|---|
| `@kleos-research/kaleidoscope` | the `kscope` command, and the launcher that picks your platform's binary |
| one platform package, below | the memory engine as object code, with the setup work `kscope init` does compiled into it |

npm installs the platform package that matches your machine and skips the other
three.

      MachinePlatform package

There is no install hook, no download at install time, no compiler step and no
source build. Installing puts files on your disk and does nothing else.

## Licences

The memory engine is proprietary object code, and its source is not in the
package. Everything around it is Apache-2.0: the command-line tool, both SDKs,
every integration and the agent skill.

## Signing

Nothing is signed for release. There is no Apple signing and no notarisation,
and the native code is ad-hoc signed only. It is on the list to fix.

## There is no Python package

`kscope-memory` on PyPI is a 0.0.0 placeholder whose own summary says it is not
yet released. `kaleidoscope-memory` was planned and never registered — if you
find that name, it is not us.

Next: Getting started activates your key and gives a project a memory.

What works today · Platforms ·
Release notes

# Privacy

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/privacy/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Your memory stays on your machine. One request leaves it, and your memory is
not in it.

## What never leaves your machine

Storing, searching and reading your memory all work offline. The embedding
model is bundled and runs locally, so nothing in that path calls a model
provider.

None of this goes anywhere: memory content, the queries you ran, the results
you got back, memory IDs, graph data, local paths, vault locations, and any
credentials you have stored locally.

## The one network request

Kaleidoscope checks that your key is still valid. The check sends three things.

| Sent | Where it travels |
|---|---|
| Your key | the request's authorization header |
| The platform you are running on | the request body |
| The version of the component that makes the check | the request body |

The body is those two fields and no more: no memory content, no queries, no
results, no file paths. The check runs in the background and caches its answer.

## Sign-in

There is no account to create and no sign-in.

If sign-in ships, it manages your account and your devices. Memory content,
queries, results, memory IDs, graph data, local paths and vault locations are
excluded from the account protocol, and the account client rejects those
fields — and any absolute local path — before anything would leave your
machine.

The refresh credential goes to the operating system's own credential store: the
login Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, the Secret Service on
Linux.

Account and devices has the rest, including why an unsigned
build can re-prompt for your login password on macOS.

## This documentation site

These pages are static files served by GitHub Pages. They set no cookies and
carry no analytics, and the only scripts on them make the navigation work.
Nothing here reads a vault, a profile, or any local memory.

Your browser keeps two things, neither of them sent anywhere: your
light-or-dark theme choice, in local storage, and the navigation sidebar's
state, in session storage, which your browser discards when you close the tab.

The pages make one third-party request. The typefaces come from Google Fonts
(`fonts.googleapis.com` and `fonts.gstatic.com`), so Google receives the request
metadata a font fetch carries, including your IP address. Block it and you lose
the typefaces.

## Hosted memory

There is no hosted service, no endpoint or API to send your memory to, and no
waitlist. If that changes it will be a separate product with its own terms, and
no local profile or sign-in will opt you into it.

---

The current version is 0.0.5. It was published to npm as
`@kleos-research/kaleidoscope`, alongside a package for each of the four
platforms it is built for — macOS on Apple Silicon and x86_64, Linux on arm64
and x86_64. It gives you the `kscope` command, it needs a key to run, and
nothing in it is signed for release. Install is how you get
it.

There is no entry below for it, and none for the versions before it. Notes begin
with the next version, and from there every version will be listed here, newest
first.

Each entry will say which platforms that version runs on, which editor and agent
versions it was checked against, what changed, what broke or was removed, whether
anything you already have needs to be moved or reconfigured, and any security
fixes it carries.

Until the second one, Status is the current picture: what is
available, what is not, and what has actually been run.
